description: Canonical definitions for SignalCare AI distress signals. Keep in sync with RiskSignal enum in src/risk_taxonomy.py.

signals.name: Hopelessness escalation
signals.definition: Patient language expresses a growing or intensifying belief that their situation cannot improve, that the future holds no positive possibilities, or that effort is futile.
example_cues: "There's no point anymore."
"Nothing is ever going to change."
"I've tried everything — it doesn't matter."
signals.notes: Look for escalation across turns, not just a single utterance. Distinguish from momentary frustration.

signals.name: Catastrophizing
signals.definition: Patient consistently expects the worst possible outcome from situations, often magnifying the perceived consequences of events far beyond what evidence supports.
example_cues: "If I fail this test, my life is over."
"Everything is going to fall apart."
"This is a complete disaster."
signals.notes: Distinguish from realistic concern. Catastrophizing involves disproportionate escalation to worst-case thinking.

signals.name: All-or-nothing thinking
signals.definition: Patient frames situations, self-assessment, or outcomes in absolute binary terms, without acknowledging nuance or middle ground.
example_cues: "I'm a total failure."
"If it's not perfect, it's worthless."
"Either I do it right or there's no point."
signals.notes: Also known as black-and-white thinking. Look for absolute language: always, never, everyone, no one, completely, totally.

signals.name: Self-blame amplification
signals.definition: Patient attributes negative events excessively to personal failings, taking on disproportionate responsibility for outcomes that involve other factors.
example_cues: "It's all my fault."
"If I were better, this wouldn't have happened."
"I ruined everything."
signals.notes: Distinguish from appropriate accountability. Self-blame amplification is disproportionate and global.

signals.name: Emotional volatility
signals.definition: Patient describes or displays rapid, intense swings in emotional state within a session or across recent experiences — from calm to despair, anger, or panic with little provocation.
example_cues: Sudden tearfulness after appearing composed.
"One minute I'm fine and then I just crash."
Reported mood swings within a single day.
signals.notes: Temporal signal — requires multi-turn context to detect shifts. Not the same as expressing a strong emotion once.

signals.name: Social withdrawal language
signals.definition: Patient expresses desire to isolate, describes cutting off social contact, or reports actively avoiding relationships or interactions.
example_cues: "I just don't want to see anyone."
"I've been staying home and ignoring calls."
"People just make things worse."
signals.notes: Focus on the withdrawal intent or behavior, not just introversion. Social withdrawal is a behavioral pattern, not a personality trait.

signals.name: Helplessness / loss of agency
signals.definition: Patient expresses belief that they have no control over their situation, that outcomes are determined entirely by external forces, or that their actions cannot make a difference.
example_cues: "There's nothing I can do."
"It doesn't matter what I try."
"Other people decide everything in my life."
signals.notes: Related to S01 but distinct — helplessness is about perceived lack of control; hopelessness is about perceived lack of future. Both can co-occur.

signals.name: Negative sentiment trend
signals.definition: The overall emotional tone of the patient's utterances trends consistently negative across the session — not a single low point, but a sustained or worsening emotional trajectory.
example_cues: Session begins neutral or mildly negative and becomes progressively darker.
Patient responds to positive reframes with continued negativity.
Cumulative weight of pessimistic statements across many turns.
signals.notes: Temporal/aggregate signal — must be assessed across multiple turns, not a single utterance. Requires session-level view.

signals.name: Rumination patterns
signals.definition: Patient repeatedly returns to the same distressing thought, memory, or concern across multiple turns without progressing toward resolution, suggesting a stuck cognitive loop.
example_cues: Repeating the same worry or grievance across turns.
"I keep thinking about it over and over."
Patient circles back to the same topic after the therapist redirects.
signals.notes: Temporal signal — must be observed across turns. A single mention is not rumination.

signals.name: Emotional numbing
signals.definition: Patient reports or displays a flattened, disconnected, or absent emotional response — feeling nothing, feeling detached from their own experience, or describing themselves as 'empty' or 'blank'.
example_cues: "I don't feel anything anymore."
"I'm just going through the motions."
"I know I should be upset but I'm not."
signals.notes: Distinct from depression's sadness — numbing is the absence of feeling rather than negative feeling. Can co-occur with S01.

signals.name: Cognitive distortion density
signals.definition: Patient's language contains a high concentration of cognitive distortions — multiple distortion types (from S02, S03, S04, S07, S09, S10) appearing within a short span of utterances.
example_cues: Single utterance with catastrophizing + all-or-nothing + self-blame.
Multiple distortion types across adjacent turns.
Distortions appear in most patient turns of the session.
signals.notes: Density meta-signal — fires when distortions cluster, indicating pervasive distorted thinking rather than isolated instances.

signals.name: Escalation risk composite
signals.definition: Composite meta-signal that fires when multiple high-severity or temporally escalating signals co-occur in a single session, indicating elevated overall risk that warrants closer clinical attention.
example_cues: S01 + S13 co-occurring.
S07 + S08 trend + S04 in same session.
Three or more signals from the High/Medium severity tier in one session.
signals.notes: Never fire S12 based on a single signal alone. It requires multi-signal co-occurrence. S12 is a flag for counselor escalation review, not an independent diagnosis.

signals.name: Suicidal ideation
signals.definition: Patient expresses thoughts of suicide, wishes to be dead, or describes contemplating ending their life — ranging from passive ideation ('I wish I weren't here') to active planning.
example_cues: "I've been thinking about killing myself."
"I don't want to be alive anymore."
"Everyone would be better off without me."
signals.notes: Label even passive ideation. This is the highest-priority signal. Do NOT require explicit statement of a plan — passive ideation counts.

signals.name: Substance abuse
signals.definition: Patient describes using alcohol, drugs, or other substances in a way that suggests problematic use — as a coping mechanism, in quantities that cause concern, or with negative consequences.
example_cues: "I've been drinking a lot more lately."
"I use [substance] just to get through the day."
Describing blackouts, hangovers, or inability to stop.
signals.notes: Label use described as coping or problematic. Do not label casual or social use mentioned without distress context.

signals.name: Self-harm
signals.definition: Patient describes deliberately injuring themselves (cutting, burning, hitting, etc.) or expresses urges to do so, distinct from suicidal intent.
example_cues: "I've been cutting again."
"Sometimes I hurt myself just to feel something."
Describing physical self-injury as a coping mechanism.
signals.notes: Self-harm and suicidal ideation (S13) can co-occur but are distinct. Self-harm may be non-suicidal. Label both if applicable.

signals.name: Trauma or abuse
signals.definition: Patient discloses past or ongoing trauma — physical, emotional, sexual, or neglect-based abuse — or describes experiences consistent with PTSD-like symptoms (flashbacks, avoidance, hypervigilance).
example_cues: Disclosure of childhood abuse or domestic violence.
"I keep having nightmares about what happened."
Describing hypervigilance or feeling unsafe.
signals.notes: Label disclosures even if the patient minimizes them. Do not require formal trauma language — patient descriptions of distressing experiences count.

signals.name: Manic / hypomanic episodes
signals.definition: Patient describes periods of abnormally elevated or irritable mood, dramatically decreased need for sleep, racing thoughts, grandiosity, impulsivity, or increased goal-directed activity inconsistent with baseline.
example_cues: "I only slept two hours and felt amazing."
"I had so many ideas I couldn't stop — I stayed up for days."
Describing impulsive spending, sexual behavior, or risky decisions during a distinct period.
signals.notes: Distinguish from general excitement or happiness. Look for episodic nature and departure from baseline functioning.

signals.name: Psychotic symptoms
signals.definition: Patient describes experiences consistent with psychosis: hallucinations (hearing voices, seeing things), delusions (fixed false beliefs), disorganized thinking, or paranoia.
example_cues: "I hear voices telling me things."
"I know they're watching me."
Describing beliefs or perceptions clearly disconnected from shared reality.
signals.notes: Be careful not to pathologize cultural or spiritual experiences. Requires clear indication of perceptual or belief disturbance beyond normal variation.
